concept_html:
pyproject.toml states what your project accepts: pandas>=3.0,<4. A lock file records what was installed: pandas 3.0.6, numpy 2.4.6, and every indirect dependency, each with a file hash. You need both.

  • The ranges in pyproject.toml say which versions your code supports. Keep them honest: a lower bound you have tested, an upper bound at the next major version when the library breaks things across majors.
  • The lock file makes every install identical: your laptop, a colleague's, CI and the scheduled job. Commit it.

With uv (examples use uv 0.8):

uv lock                  # resolve pyproject.toml ranges, write uv.lock
uv sync --locked         # install exactly uv.lock; fail if it is out of date
uv lock --upgrade-package pandas   # move one package on purpose

uv sync --locked exits with an error when pyproject.toml has changed since the lock was written: "The lockfile at uv.lock needs to be updated, but --locked was provided." Use it in CI, so a dependency change without a new lock fails the build instead of resolving something new on the runner.

Without uv, pip-compile --generate-hashes (pip-tools) writes a fully pinned requirements.txt with hashes, and pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt refuses any file whose hash differs.

pip freeze > requirements.txt is a weaker substitute. It lists what happens to be in your environment, including packages you installed by hand for a one-off test, with no hashes and no record of why each is there.

Upgrade on purpose: one dependency at a time, on a branch, with tests. Record the reason in the commit message. Never let a fresh install pick up new versions silently.

title: Pinned dependencies and lock files
why_html:
A forecasting job ran on a fresh container every night. requirements.txt said pandas>=2.0. The night pandas 3.0 was released, the container installed it. The job's text columns switched to the new str dtype, a .str.contains call behaved differently on missing values, and the job filtered out 6% of rows. Nobody had changed a line of code.

A committed lock file, installed with uv sync --locked, keeps the old pandas until someone upgrades it deliberately, with tests.
